title: Binary Search
description: Learn how **Binary Search** repeatedly **halves a sorted search space** and why logarithmic reduction makes searching extremely efficient.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
**Binary Search** is an efficient searching algorithm used to locate an element inside a **sorted array**.
Instead of checking elements one by one like linear search, Binary Search works efficiently by:
1.  **Finding the middle element** of the search space.
2.  **Comparing it** with the target.
3.  **Removing half** of the remaining search space.

Imagine searching for a specific page in a 1000 page book:
*  **Linear search** would check page 1, 2, 3, up to 1000 in the worst case.
*  **Binary search** opens the book to page 500, then decides whether the target page is before or after, **discarding 500 pages instantly**.
*  Then it opens to page 250 or 750, discarding another 250 pages.
*  Within 10 page turns, you have found the exact page.

This repeated halving makes Binary Search **dramatically faster than Linear Search** for large datasets.
For 1 billion items, linear search needs up to 1 billion comparisons. Binary search needs **only about 30 comparisons**.
That is the difference between 30 seconds and an instant response.

The algorithm is one of the most important examples of **Divide and Conquer thinking** because it aggressively reduces problem size at every step.
The same halving principle applies to many computational problems beyond just searching arrays.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Matters
sections.content:
Searching is one of the most common operations in computing.
Large systems constantly locate records, files, usernames, database entries, and indexed values.
Every time you type a query into Google, search for a contact on your phone, or filter products on Amazon, **a search algorithm is working behind the scenes**.

Sequential searching becomes expensive as datasets grow larger.
*  Consider a database with 1 billion records.
*  Linear search would need up to 1 billion comparisons, which is impractical for interactive use.
*  Binary Search **improves scalability by repeatedly eliminating half of the remaining search space** after every comparison.

For 1 billion records, binary search needs only about 30 comparisons.
This is why **databases use indexes** that allow binary search.
The same halving principle is used in debugging tools like git bisect to find which commit introduced a bug, and in numerical analysis to find roots of equations.

Binary Search demonstrates Divide and Conquer thinking clearly and introduces **logarithmic growth behavior**, which is one of the most important concepts in algorithm analysis.
Understanding binary search prepares you for more advanced data structures like binary search trees and balanced trees.

sections.title: Important Requirement — Sorted Data
sections.content:
Binary Search **only works correctly when the data is sorted** in non-decreasing order.
This is not optional. It is a fundamental requirement of the algorithm.
The sorting requirement is what **enables the halving strategy**.

For example, the array `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]` allows the algorithm to safely eliminate half of the remaining search space after each comparison because the ordering provides meaningful information.
If the target is 10 and the middle is 8, you know the target **must be to the right** because all elements to the left are less than or equal to 8.

If the array is unsorted like `[10, 2, 8, 6, 12, 4]`, comparisons lose meaning.
*  The middle might be 8, but the target 10 could be anywhere.
*  The algorithm may discard the wrong section.
*  This makes Binary Search **unreliable on unordered data**.

If you have unsorted data but want to use binary search, you must sort it first.
*  Sorting costs O(n log n) time.
*  If you only search once, linear search might be better.
*  **If you search many times, sorting once is worth it**.

sections.title: Core Idea of Binary Search
sections.content:
Binary Search repeatedly **divides the problem in half** until the target is found or no elements remain.
The core insight is that you do not need to check every element. You just need to **narrow down where the target could be**.

The algorithm executes these core steps:
1.  **Find the middle element.**
2.  **Compare it with the target.**
3.  **Remove the unnecessary half.** If the target is less than the middle, discard the right half. If greater, discard the left half.
4.  **Repeat the process** on the remaining section.

This reduction continues until the target is found or the search space becomes empty.
At that point, the algorithm returns -1 or another **not found sentinel**.

Every step dramatically shrinks the remaining workload.
For an array of size n, the maximum number of steps is roughly **log base 2 of n plus 1**.
This logarithmic growth is what makes binary search so powerful. It turns exponential search spaces into manageable ones.

sections.title: Understanding the Search Pointers
sections.content:
Binary Search commonly uses three important positions called **low, high, and mid**.
These pointers define and navigate the current search range:
*  The **low pointer** marks the beginning of the search range.
*  The **high pointer** marks the end of the search range.
*  The **mid pointer** represents the middle element currently being checked.

Initially, low starts at index 0 and high starts at the last index. The midpoint is calculated from the current low and high positions.

The search range is from low to high inclusive.
*  The algorithm continues while **low is less than or equal to high**.
*  When low equals high, only one element is left to check.
*  When low becomes greater than high, the search space is empty and the target is not found.

Pointer updates dictate the search space reduction:
1.  If the target is greater than the middle, **set low to mid plus 1** to search the right half.
2.  If the target is less than the middle, **set high to mid minus 1** to search the left half.
3.  These pointer updates must be precise. Using mid instead of mid plus 1 or mid minus 1 can cause infinite loops.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Example
sections.content:
Suppose we search for the number 11 inside the sorted array `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15]`.

**Step 1:**
*  Initially, low is 0 and high is 6.
*  The **midpoint is index 3**, which has value 7.
*  Compare 7 with 11. Since 11 is greater than 7, we eliminate the entire left half.
*  **Set low to 4**. The remaining search space is indices 4 to 6 with values `[9, 11, 15]`.

**Step 2:**
*  Now low is 4 and high is 6.
*  The **midpoint is index 5**, which has value 11.
*  Compare 11 with 11. They are equal.
*  The target is found at index 5. The **algorithm returns 5**. Only 2 comparisons were needed.

**Not-Found Scenario:**
*  If we search for a value that does not exist, like 10, the algorithm would continue until low becomes greater than high.
*  After checking index 4 which has 9 and index 5 which has 11, low becomes 5 and high becomes 4, so **low is greater than high**.
*  The algorithm returns -1.

This example demonstrates how Binary Search rapidly reduces the amount of work through **repeated halving**. From 7 elements, only 2 comparisons were needed. For 1 million elements, only about 20 comparisons would be needed.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Is Fast
sections.content:
The most powerful feature of Binary Search is **search space reduction**.
Every comparison removes 50 percent of the remaining elements. This is **geometric reduction**.
After k comparisons, at most n divided by 2 to the power of k elements remain.

Suppose a dataset contains 1 million elements:
*  After 1 comparison, about 500,000 remain.
*  After 2 comparisons, about 250,000 remain.
*  After 3 comparisons, about 125,000 remain.
*  After 10 comparisons, about 977 remain.
*  After 20 comparisons, about 1 remains.

**The workload shrinks extremely quickly.**
For 1 billion elements, only about 30 comparisons are needed. Linear search would need up to 1 billion comparisons. That is **30 million times more work**.
The chart below compares O(log n) for binary search with O(n) for linear search and O(n squared) for quadratic algorithms.

This repeated halving creates **logarithmic growth**, which scales very efficiently for large inputs.
In fact, O(log n) is so efficient that for all practical input sizes up to 2 to the power of 100, the number of operations is under 100.
This is why binary search is preferred for large datasets.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
Binary Search implementations must correctly update search pointers and repeatedly reduce the search space until the target is found or no valid range remains.
The **iterative version is most common** because it uses constant extra memory and avoids recursion limits.

The iterative implementation uses a while loop with the condition **low less than or equal to high**:
*  Inside the loop, it calculates mid as low plus high divided by 2 using integer division.
*  It then checks if the middle element equals the target. If so, it returns the index.
*  If the target is greater, it **sets low to mid plus 1**.
*  If the target is less, it **sets high to mid minus 1**.

The recursive implementation is more elegant but uses O(log n) stack space.
*  It follows the same logic but **calls itself on the left or right half** instead of using a loop.
*  The base case is when low is greater than high, in which case it returns -1.

Edge cases to test include empty arrays, single element arrays, targets smaller than all elements, targets larger than all elements, and arrays with duplicate values.
Binary search returns **any matching index** when duplicates exist, not necessarily the first or last.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Binary Search achieves **O(log n) average-case and worst-case complexity** because the search space halves during every iteration.
*  After k comparisons, the search space size is at most n divided by 2 to the power of k.
*  The algorithm stops when the search space is empty.
*  The maximum k needed satisfies n divided by 2 to the power of k is less than 1, which means k is greater than log base 2 of n.

Time Complexity breakdown:
*  The best case is **O(1)**, which occurs when the target is exactly the middle element of the array. Only 1 comparison is needed.
*  The average case is also O(log n). For random targets in a random sorted array, the expected number of comparisons is about log base 2 of n minus 1.

Space complexity breakdown:
*  Space complexity is **O(1)** for iterative implementations because only three integer variables low, high, and mid are needed regardless of input size.
*  Recursive implementations use **O(log n) auxiliary space** because each recursive call adds a stack frame.
*  For n equals 1 billion, log base 2 of n is about 30 stack frames, which is fine.
*  In Python, the recursion limit is about 1000, so binary search recursion depth is safe.

Compared to linear search, binary search is exponentially faster for large n.
For n equals 1 million, linear search needs up to 1 million comparisons while binary search needs about 20 comparisons. That is **50,000 times faster**.

sections.title: Binary Search vs Linear Search
sections.content:
Linear Search and Binary Search represent two fundamentally different approaches to searching.
*  Linear Search works on unsorted data and scans sequentially. It takes **O(n)** time in the worst case.
*  Binary Search requires sorted data but takes **O(log n)** time.

Speed Comparison:
*  For n equals 1 million, linear search needs up to 1 million comparisons. Binary search needs about 20 comparisons. That is **50,000 times faster**.
*  For n equals 1 billion, linear search needs up to 1 billion comparisons. Binary search needs about 30 comparisons. That is **33 million times faster**.

However, binary search has strict requirements:
1.  The data must be sorted. If the data is unsorted, you must sort it first. **Sorting costs O(n log n) time**.
2.  For a single search, linear search O(n) may be faster than sorting plus binary search O(n log n plus log n).
3.  For many searches, sorting once is worth it.
4.  Binary search also requires random access to elements, like an array.
5.  It **does not work efficiently on linked lists** because finding the middle element takes O(n) time. Linear search works fine on linked lists.

For very small n less than 50, the difference is negligible and linear search may be simpler.

sections.title: Recursive Binary Search
sections.content:
Binary Search can also be implemented recursively.
Instead of using loops, the function **repeatedly calls itself on smaller search ranges**.
Each recursive call handles a reduced portion of the array until the target is found or the search range becomes invalid.

The recursive structure mirrors the mathematical definition of divide and conquer:
1.  The **base case** is when low is greater than high, which means the target is not found. The function returns -1.
2.  If the middle element equals the target, it returns the index.
3.  If the target is greater than the middle, it recursively calls itself on the right half with **low set to mid plus 1**.
4.  If the target is less, it recursively calls itself on the left half with **high set to mid minus 1**.

Recursive implementations reinforce the idea of recursive decomposition in Divide and Conquer algorithms. They are often shorter and more elegant.
However, they use **O(log n) stack space**, while iterative versions use O(1) space.
For most practical purposes, the iterative version is preferred due to its constant space usage and better performance.

Recursive binary search is excellent for learning and for problems that naturally fit recursion, like searching in a binary search tree.
The call depth is log n, which is very shallow. For n equals 1 billion, depth is about 30, well within recursion limits.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: Maintaining sorted data may **require additional work**.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Binary Search appears in many real-world systems:

*  **Databases:** They use **indexes that allow binary search** to locate records quickly. When you query SELECT WHERE id equals 12345, the database uses an index that enables O(log n) lookup instead of scanning millions of rows.
*  **Search Engines:** Google uses **inverted indexes**. When you search for a word, the engine finds the word in its sorted dictionary using binary search, then retrieves the list of documents containing that word.
*  **Version Control:** Debugging systems like **git bisect** use binary search to find which commit introduced a bug. You mark a known good commit and a known bad commit, and Git repeatedly checks the middle commit, asking you whether it is good or bad, halving the search space each time.
*  **UI Features:** **Autocomplete systems** use binary search on a sorted dictionary to find words starting with a given prefix.
*  **Low-Level Systems:** Compilers use binary search in symbol tables. Networking uses binary search in congestion control algorithms.

Many modern systems rely on Binary Search because logarithmic growth remains efficient even for extremely large datasets.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using Binary Search on unsorted arrays
subsections.content:
Binary Search **requires ordered data**.
Without sorting, comparisons cannot safely eliminate sections of the array. The algorithm will produce incorrect results, sometimes returning -1 when the target exists or returning an index of a wrong element. **Always sort the array first** or ensure the data is already sorted.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect midpoint calculation
subsections.content:
Poor midpoint logic may create infinite loops, skipped elements, or incorrect search behavior.
Use integer division with **//** in Python. In languages with integer overflow, use **low plus (high minus low) divided by 2** instead of (low plus high) divided by 2.

subsections.title: Mistake: Forgetting pointer updates
subsections.content:
If the low or high pointers are not updated correctly, the search range may never shrink properly, causing **infinite loops**.
Set low to mid plus 1 when searching the right half. Set high to mid minus 1 when searching the left half. **Never set low to mid or high to mid** because that would not exclude the already checked middle element.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The algorithm repeatedly **divides the search space in half**.
Binary Search uses **low, high, and mid pointers**.
Each comparison **removes half of the remaining work**.
Divide and Conquer thinking **enables scalable searching**.
